source.title: BLUEFIN: Benchmarking LLM Agents on Financial Spreadsheets

issues.problem: The blurb asks "Why did the authors remove a separate 'structural completeness' rubric category, and how does the final rubric still catch a badly structured workbook?" Block 7, directly above, answers both parts almost word for word: "over-rewarded copying the reference template and penalised valid alternative builds. Structure is instead captured indirectly…". The reader can paraphrase the previous paragraph without understanding the point.
issues.suggestion: Turn it into an application question. For example: "Imagine an agent builds a correct DCF with a different tab layout from the reference. Explain how BLUEFIN's rubric treats it, and why a structural-completeness section would have treated it worse." Keep required criteria on the over-rewarding of template copying and on structure being captured through the other categories. Alternatively, move the exercise after another explanation block so it calls on retrieval rather than short-term memory.

issues.problem: "Questions are deliberately of the form 'if these inputs change, what happens to this output?'" presents this as true of every interrogation task. The paper says only that the authors identified inputs feeding multi-step calculation chains and "prioritized these examples", and that "many tasks require agents to update spreadsheet assumptions".
issues.suggestion: Reword to: "The authors prioritised questions whose answer depends on inputs that propagate through multi-step calculation chains; many ask what happens to an output when assumptions change."

issues.problem: "It is still telling that a model at about 49% on the rubric can be a useful starting point three times out of four." The 49% is Opus's held-out score, but the utility study rated outputs from the release (public) set. On that set Opus scored 58.4% (Table 5). The comparison mixes two task sets.
issues.suggestion: Either compare with the public-set score ("a model scoring about 58% on the public set's rubric was judged a useful starting point three times out of four") or drop the numeric comparison and say only that a usable starting point does not require a high rubric score.
